en: Such indeed were the precautions of human wisdom. The next thing was to seek means of propitiating the gods, and recourse was had to the Sibylline books, by the direction of which prayers were offered to Vulcanus, Ceres, and Proserpina. Juno, too, was entreated by the matrons, first, in the Capitol, then on the nearest part of the coast, whence water was procured to sprinkle the fane and image of the goddess. And there were sacred banquets and nightly vigils celebrated by married women.
title: Tacitus, Annals 15.44: Nero, the fire of Rome and the Christians
author: Tacitus

en: But all human efforts, all the lavish gifts of the emperor, and the propitiations of the gods, did not banish the sinister belief that the conflagration was the result of an order. Consequently, to get rid of the report, Nero fastened the guilt and inflicted the most exquisite tortures on a class hated for their abominations, called Christians by the populace.
title: Tacitus, Annals 15.44: Nero, the fire of Rome and the Christians
author: Tacitus

en: Christus, from whom the name had its origin, suffered the extreme penalty during the reign of Tiberius at the hands of one of our procurators, Pontius Pilatus, and a most mischievous superstition, thus checked for the moment, again broke out not only in Judæa, the first source of the evil, but even in Rome, where all things hideous and shameful from every part of the world find their centre and become popular.
title: Tacitus, Annals 15.44: Nero, the fire of Rome and the Christians
author: Tacitus

en: Accordingly, an arrest was first made of all who pleaded guilty; then, upon their information, an immense multitude was convicted, not so much of the crime of firing the city, as of hatred against mankind. Mockery of every sort was added to their deaths. Covered with the skins of beasts, they were torn by dogs and perished, or were nailed to crosses, or were doomed to the flames and burnt, to serve as a nightly illumination, when daylight had expired.
title: Tacitus, Annals 15.44: Nero, the fire of Rome and the Christians
author: Tacitus

en: Nero offered his gardens for the spectacle, and was exhibiting a show in the circus, while he mingled with the people in the dress of a charioteer or stood aloft on a car. Hence, even for criminals who deserved extreme and exemplary punishment, there arose a feeling of compassion; for it was not, as it seemed, for the public good, but to glut one man’s cruelty, that they were being destroyed.
title: Tacitus, Annals 15.44: Nero, the fire of Rome and the Christians
author: Tacitus

en: Since the Jews constantly made disturbances at the instigation of Chrestus, he expelled them from Rome. He allowed the envoys of the Germans to sit in the orchestra, led by their naïve self-confidence; for when they had been taken to the seats occupied by the common people and saw the Parthian and Armenian envoys sitting with the senate, they moved of their own accord to the same part of the theatre, protesting that their merits and rank were no whit inferior.
title: Suetonius, Claudius 25.4: the Jews expelled from Rome 'at the instigation of Chrestus'
author: Suetonius

en: During his reign many abuses were severely punished and put down, and no fewer new laws were made: a limit was set to expenditures; the public banquets were confined to a distribution of food; the sale of any kind of cooked viands in the taverns was forbidden, with the exception of pulse and vegetables, whereas before every sort of dainty was exposed for sale. Punishment was inflicted on the Christians, a class of men given to a new and mischievous superstition. He put an end to the diversions of the chariot drivers, who from immunity of long standing claimed the right of ranging at large and amusing themselves by cheating and robbing the people. The pantomimic actors and their partisans were banished from the city.
title: Suetonius, Nero 16.2: 'punishment was inflicted on the Christians'
author: Suetonius

en: 1-3 Now the lord once decided to set off for the mountain where the man lives; Lord Gilgameš decided to set off for the mountain where the man lives. He spoke to his slave Enkidu:
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 8-12 His slave Enkidu answered him: "My lord, if today you are going to set off into the mountains, Utu should know about it from us. (1 ms. adds: If you are going to to set off into the Mountains of Cedar-felling, Utu should know about it from us.) Utu, youthful Utu, should know about it from us. A decision that concerns the mountains is Utu's business. A decision that concerns the Mountains of Cedar-felling is the business of youthful Utu. Utu should know about it from us."
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 17-18 "Utu, I am going to set off into the mountains! May you be my helper! I am going to set off into the Mountains of Cedar-felling! May you be my helper!"
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 19-20 From heaven Utu replied to him: "Young man, you are noble already in your own right -- but what would you want with the mountains?"
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 21-33 "Utu, I have something to say to you -- a word in your ear! I greet you -- please pay attention! In my city people are dying, and hearts are full of distress. People are lost -- that fills me with (1 ms. adds: wretched) dismay. I craned my neck over the city wall: corpses in the water make the river almost overflow. That is what I see. That will happen to me too -- that is the way things go. No one is tall enough to reach heaven; no one can reach wide enough to stretch over the mountains. Since a man cannot pass beyond the final end of life, I want to set off into the mountains, to establish my renown there. Where renown can be established there, I will establish my renown; and where no renown can be established there, I shall establish the renown of the gods."
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 34-47 Utu accepted his tears as a fitting gift. As befits a compassionate person, he turned to him full of compassion: "Now there are seven warriors, sons of a single mother. The first, their eldest brother, has lion's paws and eagle's talons. The second is a …… snake, ……. The third is a dragon snake, ……. The fourth blazes with fire ……. The fifth is a …… snake, ……. The sixth (1 ms. adds: , a shackle that …… the rebel lands in the hills,) beats at the flanks of the mountains like a battering flood (1 ms. has instead: , floodwater that destroys all). The seventh …… flashes like lightning, and no one can deflect it (1 ms. has instead: its power). (1 ms. adds 4 lines: (4 lines fragmentary)) (another ms. adds instead 6 lines: (2 lines fragmentary) …… kingship ……. Nisaba has bestowed …… on you in addition. They ……, and know the routes on earth. They will help you find the …… of the way.) They should guide you to the place in the mountains where the boats have to be pulled from the water! The warrior, youthful Utu, gave these seven to Gilgameš. (3 mss. have instead the line, placed after line 43: These seven the warrior, youthful Utu, gave to Lord Gilgameš.) The feller of cedars was filled with joy; Lord Gilgameš was filled with joy."
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 48-51 In his city he had the horn sounded for single men; similarly for two together he made them call out. "Let him who has a household go to his household! Let him who has a mother go to his mother! Let bachelor males, types like me, (4 mss. add: -- fifty of them --) join me at my side!"
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 52-60 Whoever had a household went to his household. Whoever had a mother went to his mother. Bachelor males, types like him -- there were fifty -- joined him at his side. He made his way to the blacksmith's, and had them cast …… weapons and axes, the strength of warriors. Then he made his way to the deeply shaded plantations, where he had ebony trees felled, and ḫalub trees, apricot trees, and box trees. He …… to his fellow-citizens who were going with him. (1 ms. adds: Warriors, sons of a single mother …….) The first, their eldest brother, has lion's paws and eagle's claws. They will guide him to the place in the mountains where the boats have to be pulled from the water.
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 68-75 Gilgameš …… was overcome by sleep, and it affected Enkidu …… as a powerful longing. His fellow-citizens who had come with him flailed around at his feet like puppies. Enkidu awoke from his dream, shuddering from his sleep. He rubbed his eyes; there was eery silence everywhere. He touched Gilgameš, but could not rouse him. He spoke to him, but he did not reply.
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 76-84 "You who have gone to sleep, you who have gone to sleep! Gilgameš, young lord of Kulaba, how long will you sleep for? The mountains are becoming indistinct as the shadows fall across them; the evening twilight lies over them. Proud Utu has already gone to the bosom of his mother Ningal. Gilgameš, how long will you sleep for? The sons of your city who came with you should not have to wait at the foot of the hills. Their own mothers should not have to twine string in the square of your city."
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 85-89 He thrust that into his right ear; he covered him with his aggressive words as if with a cloth (1 ms. adds: , laid them out like linen). He gathered (3 mss. have instead: picked up) in his hand a cloth with thirty shekels of oil on it and smothered (1 ms. has instead: rubbed) it over Gilgameš's chest. Then Gilgameš stood up like a bull on the great earth. Bending his neck downwards, he yelled at him:
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 90-91 "By the life of my own mother Ninsumun and of my father, holy Lugalbanda! Am I to become again as if I were slumbering still on the lap of my own mother Ninsumun?"
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 92-95 A second time he spoke to him: "By the life of my own mother Ninsumun and of my father, holy Lugalbanda! Until I discover whether that person was a human or a god, I shall not direct back to the city my steps which I have directed to the mountains."
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 96-97 The slave, trying to ameliorate the situation, trying to make life appear more attractive, answered his master:
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 98-106 "My master, you have not yet really seen that person, he should not vex you. -- But he vexes me -- me, who have seen him before. His pugnacious mouth is a dragon's maw; his face is a lion's grimace. His chest is like a raging flood; no one dare approach (1 ms. has instead: can escape from) his brow, which devours the reedbeds. (2 mss. adds 1 line: A man-eating lion, he never wipes away the blood from his slaver.) (1 ms. adds instead 5 lines: (1 line fragmentary) …… a lion eating a corpse, he never wipes away the blood (3 lines fragmentary)) Travel on, my master, up into the mountains! -- but I shall travel back to the city. If I say to your mother about you "He is alive!", she will laugh. But afterwards I shall say to her about you "He is dead!", and she will certainly weep over you (1 ms. has instead: bitterly)." (1 ms. adds: …… replied to ……:)
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 107-116 "Look, Enkidu, two people together will not perish! A grappling-pole does not sink! No one can cut through a three-ply cloth! Water cannot wash someone away from a wall! Fire in a reed house cannot be extinguished! You help me, and I will help you -- what can anyone do against us then? When it sank, when it sank, when the Magan boat sank, when the magilum barge sank, then at least the life-saving grappling-pole of the boat was rescued (1 ms. has instead: was not allowed to sink)! Come on, let's get after him and get a sight of him!"
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 117-119 "If we go after him, there will be terror! There will be terror. Turn back! There will be blood! There wil be blood! Turn back!"
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 120 "Whatever you may think -- come on, let's get after him!"
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 121-125 Before a man can approach within even sixty times six yards, Ḫuwawa has already reached his house among the cedars. When he looks at someone, it is the look of death. When he shakes his head at someone, it is a gesture full of reproach. (1 ms. adds: When he speaks to someone, he should not prolong his words:) "You may still be a young man, but you will never again return to the city of your mother who bore you!"
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 126-129 Fear and terror spread through his (1 ms. has instead: Gilgameš's) sinews and his feet. He could not move (?) his feet on the ground; the big toenails of his feet stuck …… to the path (?). At his side …….
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 130-135 (Ḫuwawa addressed Gilgameš:) "So come on now, you heroic bearer of a sceptre of wide-ranging power! Noble glory of the gods, angry bull standing ready for a fight! Your mother knew well how to bear sons, and your nurse knew well how to nourish children on the breast! Don't be afraid, rest your hand on the ground!"
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 145-148 Then Ḫuwawa handed over to him his first terror. Gilgameš's fellow-citizens who had come with him began to lop off the branches and bundle them together, so as to lay them down at the foot of the hills.
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 149-151 When Ḫuwawa had finally handed over to him his seventh terror, Gilgameš found himself beside Ḫuwawa. He went up to him gradually (1 ms. has instead: ……) from behind, as one does with a …… snake. He made as if to kiss him, but then punched him on the cheek with his fist.
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 153-157 He tugged at Gilgameš's hand. (4 mss. have instead: "Gilgameš, let me go!") "I want to talk to Utu!" "Utu, I never knew a mother who bore me, nor a father who brought me up! I was born in the mountains -- you brought me up! Yet Gilgameš swore to me by heaven, by earth, and by the mountains."
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 158-160 Ḫuwawa clutched at Gilgameš's hand, and prostrated himself before him. Then Gilgameš's noble heart took pity on him. Gilgameš addressed Enkidu (3 mss. have instead: He addressed his slave Enkidu):
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 161-162 "Enkidu, let the captured bird run away home! Let the captured man return to his mother's embrace!"
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 163-174 Enkidu replied to Gilgameš (2 mss. have instead: His slave Enkidu replied): "Come on now, you heroic bearer of a sceptre of wide-ranging power! Noble glory of the gods, angry bull standing ready for a fight! Young Lord Gilgameš, cherished in Unug, your mother knew well how to bear sons, and your nurse knew well how to nourish children! -- One so exalted and yet so lacking in understanding (1 ms. has instead: judgment) will be devoured by fate without him ever understanding that fate. The very idea that a captured bird should run away home, or a captured man should return to his mother's embrace! -- Then you yourself would never get back to the mother-city that bore you! (1 ms. adds: A captured warrior set free! A captured high priestess …… to the ĝipar! A captured gudug priest restored to his wig of hair! …… ever, ever ……? (2 lines fragmentary) …… his attention to his words …….)"
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 175-177 Ḫuwawa addressed Enkidu: "Enkidu, you speak such hateful (1 ms. adds: hostile) words against me to him! You hireling, who are hired for your keep! You who follow along after him -- you speak such hateful words to him. (2 mss. have instead: why do you speak such hateful words to him?)" (1 ms. adds: (2 lines fragmentary))
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 178-180 As Ḫuwawa spoke thus to him, Enkidu, full of rage and anger, cut his throat (2 mss. from Nibru have instead: they cut his throat). He put (1 ms. has instead: He chucked) (the same 2 mss. from Nibru have instead: They put) his head in a leather bag.
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 181-186 They entered before Enlil. After they had kissed the ground before Enlil, they threw the leather bag down, tipped out his head, and placed it before Enlil. When Enlil saw the head of Ḫuwawa, he spoke angrily to Gilgameš: (instead of lines 181-186, 1 ms. has: They brought it before Enlil and Ninlil. When Enlil approached (?), …… went out the window (?), and Ninlil went out ……. When Enlil with Ninlil had returned (?),)
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 193-199 (The ms. tradition for lines 193-199 is extremely confused about the order in which the various auras are assigned; the following sequence is a compromise:) He gave Ḫuwawa's first aura to the fields. He gave his second aura to the rivers. He gave his third aura to the reedbeds. He gave his fourth aura to the lions. He gave his fifth aura to the palace (1 ms. has instead: debt slaves). He gave his sixth aura to the forests (1 ms. has instead: the hills). He gave his seventh aura to Nungal(the goddess of prisoners) .
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)

en: 200 …… his terror …… (1 ms. or possibly 2 mss. have instead: …… the rest of the auras …… Gilgameš …….)
title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)

en: 1-39 After the kingship descended from heaven, the kingship was in Eridug. In Eridug, Alulim became king; he ruled for 28800 years. en: 1 [O my] sagacious [brother], come, let me tell you, 2 The distress [I have seen, time and again], I would recount to you. 3 Such deep misery [as has befallen me, may it weigh heavy] on your feelings, 4 [In …] most distressful, I will always sing your praises: 5 Where be the man of insight so able to advise? 6 Whence the man of knowledge comparable to you? 7 Where else to such a counsellor my woe could I relate? 8 I was at a loss when heartache came upon me, 9 I was the youngest child when fate carried off him who begot me, 10 She who brought me into the world departed to the land of no return, 11 My father and mother left me with no one to care for me! 12 Considerate friend, what you tell is a sorrowful tale, 13 My dear friend, you have let your creativity harbor ill. 14 You make your estimable discretion feeble-minded, 15 You alter your bright expression to a scowl. 16 Our fathers are given up that they go death’s way, 17 They will cross the river Hubur, as is commanded from of old.
title: The Babylonian Theodicy (dialogue of the sufferer and his friend)
author: Saggil-kinam-ubbib

en: 18 When you survey teeming humankind all around, 19 If the poor man’s son is thriving, someone helped him prosper, 20 Who did favors for the sleek and wealthy? 21 He who looks to his god has a protector, 22 The diffident man who reveres his goddess will garner wealth. 23 My friend, your heart is a wellspring of depth unplumbed, 24 The upsurging swell of the ocean that brooks no diminishment. 25 To you, then, let me pose my questions, learn my drift, 26 Hearken to me but for a moment, hear my declaration. 27 Want and craving make up the covering of my body, 28 I have outlived my success, (my) prime is past, 29 (My) energies are gone feeble, (my) prospering is over, 30 Moaning and woe have clouded [my] features. 31 The sustenance from my tilth nowhere near suffices [me], 32 Of the fruit of the vine, what sustains humankind, I am far from having enough. 33 Can happy times be a certainty for me? I wish I knew how that might come about! 34 My well-thought-out speech is the peak of good advice, 35 Your wonted wisdom you transmute into ranting, 36 You bring forward scatter-brained, irrational […], 37 You render your choicest reasoning like a mountebank. 38 As to your everlasting, unremitting desire is […] 39 The angry god […] at the prayer of […]. 40 The estranged goddess returns upon supp[lication]. 41 If the … […] one gone astray […] forbearance, 42 Seek constantly after the […] of doing what’s right. 43 [The harshest …] will surely show kindness, 44 He will lay wide [the way], he will surely grant [you] clemency. 45 [I] have bowed [down before you], my [companion], I have absorbed [your] wisdom, 46 [I have taken to heart the] honeyed discourse of [your] lips. 47 Come, let me tell you what I understand:
title: The Babylonian Theodicy (dialogue of the sufferer and his friend)
author: Saggil-kinam-ubbib

en: 48 The onager, the wild ass, that had its fill of lush wild grasses, 49 Did it have a care for the weighty wisdom of the gods? 50 The savage lion that fed himself from the choicest meat, 51 Did it bring its flour offerings to appease a goddess’s wrath? 52 As to the rich magnate whose prosperity keeps increasing, 53 Did he weigh out precious gold to the mother goddess? 54 Have I withheld my offerings when I sacrificed to the god? 55 When blessing the regular sacrifice to my goddess, have I ever been at fault? 56 O date palm, wealth-giving tree, my treasured brother, 57 Perfect in all wisdom, O gem [of wisdom]! 58 If you are indeed fixed as the earth, the reasoning [of the gods] is far beyond (you). 59 Consider on the […] that magnificent wild ass of the plain, 60 An arrow will turn upon that one who trod every lea. 61 Come, contemplate that lion you were thinking of, livestock’s bane, 62 For the atrocities the lion committed, a pit yawns for him. 63 The well-heeled rich man who hoarded up possessions, 64 A sovereign will put him to the flames before his time.
title: The Babylonian Theodicy (dialogue of the sufferer and his friend)
author: Saggil-kinam-ubbib

en: 65 Would you wish to go the way these have gone? 66 Seek after virtue’s reward from (your) god all your days. 67 Your reasoning is a cool breeze, a breath of fresh air for humankind, 68 Most particular friend, your advice is excellent. 69 Let me put but one matter before you: 70 Those who seek not after a god can go the road of favor, 71 Those who pray to a goddess have grown poor and destitute. 72 Indeed, in my youth I heeded the will of (my) god, 73 With prayer and supplication I besought (my) goddess. 74 I bore a yoke of profitless servitude: 75 (My) god decreed (for me) penury instead of wealth. 76 A cripple rises above me, a fool is ahead of me, 77 A vile lackey is in the ascendant, I am demoted. 78 Truly, O knowledgeable one, your ponderings are devoid of common sense, 79 You have cast off truth, you have spurned divine design. 80 In your emotional state you have felt an urge to disregard observances due (your) god,
title: The Babylonian Theodicy (dialogue of the sufferer and his friend)
author: Saggil-kinam-ubbib

en: 81 You have transgressed and neglected the sound rules of (your) goddess. 82 The strategy of a god is as far [beyond (you)] as innermost heaven, 83 The command of a goddess is inaudible, […] cannot be detected. 84 Teeming humanity well understands codes of behavior, 85 But what they themselves plan for people […] 86 To instruct in the ways of a goddess […] 87 In their own minds […] 88 (no English for this line in the eBL edition)

en: 126 His back is broken, […], 127 The [most raging] fire is always put out. 128 The […]’s offspring is crushed. 129 The [most numerous …] people are scattered. 130 The midwife is convened [at the bed of the woman in labor], 131 I have paid heed to [my] god, […] 132 I have sought [to do] what […] demanded, […] 133 I will forsake home […] 134 I will crave no property […] 135 I will ignore (my) god’s regulations, [I will] trample on (his) rites. 136 I will slaughter a calf, I will […] the food, 137 I will go on the road, I will learn my way around distant places. 138 I will open up the well, I will release watercourse, 139 I will roam about the far outdoors like a fugitive. 140 I will stave off hunger by forcing entry from house to house, 141 Ravenous, I will cast about, prowling the streets. 142 Helpless, I will keep entering […]. 143 Good fortune lies afar off, my fate […].
title: The Babylonian Theodicy (dialogue of the sufferer and his friend)

en: 176 To the successors, sweet […] yoke. 177 Who among the wise is able to advise you? 178 Who among the astute is on a level with you? 179 As I look upon the land, […] its counsel, 180 What people I see, […] is more powerful. 181 The son of a king is clad [in rags], 182 The son of the destitute and naked is dressed in [fine raiment]. 183 The malster demands payment in gold, 184 While he who counted red gold shoulders a [debt]. 185 He who made do with vegetables [sates himself] at a princely banquet, 186 While the son of the magnate and rich man (has only) carob to eat. 187 The man of substance is fallen, his assets are gone. 188 (no English for this line in the eBL edition) 189 (no English for this line in the eBL edition) 190 (no English for this line in the eBL edition) 191 (no English for this line in the eBL edition)

en: 205 […] his tablet, replete with the scribal art, 206 The learned [in …] revealed to me its writing, 207 He opened my eyes to knotty and impenetrable things. 208 It seems that the course of my good fortune was fleeting, 209 I prowl the streets [looking] for [something (?)] for the emptiness of (my) mouth. 210 […] has turned away, the thoroughbred mount of a king. 211 [… the] hero among the mountains. 212 You have let your subtle mind wander, 213 […] you have driven wisdom away, 214 [You] have spurned [propriety], you have besmirched (every) code. 215 Far will be the workman’s basket from the … of the one who is lofty in […], 216 [The … lower-class man] is established as a person of importance, 217 […] he is called a scholar, 218 “His head is held high, he gets what he wants.” 219 Follow in the way of a god, observe his rites, 220 […], keep low, stand ready for good fortune!
title: The Babylonian Theodicy (dialogue of the sufferer and his friend)
author: Saggil-kinam-ubbib

en: 221 Taking the miser’s place, the scoundrel …, 222 [He who has nothing], everyone (calls him) a villain. 223 (While) he who amasses goods is (considered) tireless (and) of [...], 224 When they (sc. the people) assemble as a group, each armed with their mug, 225 Beasts […] to the disobedient … […], 226 Chapels are open, […] let them be my shelter. 227 (Although) I was attentive to the will of [(my) god, I …], 228 Should I become beastlike, … […] …
title: The Babylonian Theodicy (dialogue of the sufferer and his friend)
author: Saggil-kinam-ubbib

en: 229 Should I … my pride […] 230 Like a stand-in, my ineptitude … […] 231 I am snuffed out for lack of … […] 232 A mountain of plenty, its [yield] has withered, 233 He of wide comprehension has become like a deaf man, 234 He whose mind reached out in every direction, … […].
title: The Babylonian Theodicy (dialogue of the sufferer and his friend)
author: Saggil-kinam-ubbib

en: 235 As for the vile lackey whose good fortune you craved, 236 The verdure of the harvest, the pasture, will soon disappear. 237 The godless reprobate who is grasping of possessions, 238 The weapon of his deathblow is coming up behind him. 239 Unless you heed the will of (your) god, what will be your gain? 240 He who bears a god’s yoke will never want for food, though it may be meager. 241 Seek after the favorable breeze of the gods, 242 What you lost over a year you will recoup in a moment. 243 I have looked around in society, indications are the contrary: 244 God does not block the progress of a demon. 245 A father hauls a boat up a channel, 246 While his firstborn sprawls in bed. 247 The eldest son sprints ahead like a lion, 248 The younger brother is content to drive a donkey. 249 The heir strolls the streets like an idler, 250 The younger son makes provision for the destitute. 251 What has it profited me that I knelt before a deity? 252 It is I who must (now) bow before my inferior!
title: The Babylonian Theodicy (dialogue of the sufferer and his friend)
author: Saggil-kinam-ubbib

en: 253 The riffraff despise me, as do the rich and proud. 254 Adept scholar, master of discernment, 255 You blaspheme in the anguish of your thoughts. 256 Divine purpose is as far beyond (you) as innermost heaven, 257 It is too difficult to be conversant with, people cannot understand it. 258 Among all living creatures, the handiwork of the birth-goddess, 259 Why should offspring be completely without a say? 260 The cow’s first calf is inferior, 261 Her subsequent offspring is twice as big. 262 The first child is born a weakling, 263 The second is known as a capable warrior. 264 Even if one (tries to) apprehend divine wisdom, people cannot understand it. 265 Pay attention, my friend, learn my (next) parry, 266 Consider the well-chosen diction of my speech. 267 They extol the words of an important man who is accomplished in murder, 268 They denigrate the powerless who has committed no crime. 269 They esteem truthful the wicked to whom truth is abhorrent,
title: The Babylonian Theodicy (dialogue of the sufferer and his friend)
author: Saggil-kinam-ubbib

en: 270 They drive away the truthful man who heeds the will of god. 271 They fill the oppressor’s strongroom with treasure, 272 The larder of the helpless they empty of [his] provisions. 273 They shore up the tyrant whose all is crime, 274 They ruin the weak, they oppress the powerless. 275 And as for me, without means, a magnate harasses me. 276 Enlil, king of the gods, who created teeming humankind, 277 Majestic Ea, who pinched off their clay, 278 The queen who fashioned them, mistress Mami, 279 Gave perverse words to the human race, 280 They endowed them in perpetuity with lies and falsehood. 281 Solemnly they speak well of a rich man, 282 “He’s the king,” they say, “riches attend him.” 283 They malign a poor man as a thief, 284 They lavish malice upon him, they conspire to kill him. 285 Like a criminal, they make him suffer every evil because he has no vault. 286 They make him go numb with fear, they snuff him out like an ember. 287 You are sympathetic, my friend, be considerate of (my) misfortune. 288 Help me, see (my) distress, you should be cognizant of it. 289 I am a suppliant, versatile servant,
title: The Babylonian Theodicy (dialogue of the sufferer and his friend)
